pillar_reactions.evidence: Presented as 30-40 minutes, three to four times a week, strength/conditioning/mobility in one unit, plus short daily mobility protocols and a six-month term. The prospect already knew the modality, so it landed without friction but also without lift: 'Yeah, mean, that makes sense. That's what I would have expected. I think it would take at least three, six months to see something.' He engaged more warmly later when talking about what kettlebells had already done for him — 'just walking is easier. Walking up a hill is a little bit easier... Running feels kind of more effortless' — but that is enthusiasm for kettlebells, which he already owns, not for the offer.

What/when/how-much framing, an eight-hour eating window (noted as easy since he already skips breakfast), no snacks, and the once-a-week free meal. The prospect engaged with the content substantively — volunteering the vegetarian protein difficulty, the knowledge-work snacking habit, and the social awkwardness of eating clean around family — but asked no questions and signalled he did not think this was where his problem lay: 'No, no, I mean, I kind of know, I think what I should be eating in general. So I think that's fine.' The rep turned that into the accountability bridge rather than pressing it, which was the right move.

Clearly the pillar that mattered, and he tied it directly to the root cause he had already named himself. 'I think that's the area that, yeah, I think that's been my biggest... I think you're 100% right. I think just reaching, that's what I'm looking for, like being able to reach out and be like, hey, you know, it's not the end of the world, you know, we'll adjust.' He then supplied the reason himself: 'that's part of the reason why I'm like, okay, I can't do this all on my own all the time, just because I have these counterproductive moods that I get into.' He also volunteered agreement with the flexibility framing — 'planning for a change and being okay with that. I think that's a good point.' Worth noting that the enthusiasm cooled the moment the mechanics were made concrete at 00:42:10, when the rep clarified that check-ins are an in-app form rather than a call: the price objection follows within forty seconds.

anchors.raw: I've been doing Simple and Sinister for a little while ... I got to the 32-kilogram bell, and I was doing, you know, swings, and one-arm swings, and the get-ups ... I liked it because it's, like, good bang for buck, you know what I mean?
anchors.competitor: Simple and Sinister (Pavel Tsatsouline) — a book-priced, self-directed kettlebell programme
anchors.note: The most important anchor on the call and a direct repeat of the script gap already logged from the Badrane Hriouch call, but harder: the substitute is effectively free, he ran it successfully to a heavy bell, and its only failure was boredom rather than ineffectiveness. Every dollar of the $6,000 has to be justified against something that already worked. Nobody made that argument, and halving the price implicitly conceded it.

anchors.raw: I have no idea. Like I said, I never hired a coach. I don't even know what the price is.
anchors.note: He arrived with no reference price for coaching of any kind, which is normally an advantage for the seller — the rep can set the anchor. The rep did try ('you cannot hire a coach for every single day. That would be probably astronomical') but offered no figure, no comparison and no evidence, so the anchor never actually landed. An unanchored buyer is an opportunity that was left on the table.

anchors.raw: that's still quite a bit. I got to think about that, to be honest, because it's all virtual, right? That's the difference, you know, versus, you know, in person, right?
anchors.note: His implicit quality benchmark is a coach physically present. This sharpened immediately after the rep clarified that weekly check-ins are an in-app form and not a call, which subtracted the live human element he had been imagining. The delivery model was described accurately and honestly — and describing it accurately is what triggered the price objection.

anchors.raw: The kids go to, you know, go to a school that's pretty pricey, so... That takes up most of the budget.
anchors.note: A concrete, recurring, high-status competing commitment that the household has already prioritised, and one his wife controls jointly. Combined with 'Our situation, to be honest, is a little shaky in some ways', this is a real constraint rather than a stall. Notably it is also the exact objection the rep had role-played the wife making moments earlier and dismissed as 'blah, blah, blah'.

anchors.raw: Okay. So a thousand a month?
anchors.note: Third prospect in this batch to convert the $6,000 headline into a monthly figure within seconds of hearing it, and the second to land on exactly $1,000/month. This is now a pattern worth acting on: buyers are not processing this as a lump sum, and the rep's answer — 'Depending how you look at it. Like, if you pay it upfront, it's one-time payment. Or you can split it up' — left the frame with the prospect rather than taking it.

anchors.raw: you guys have done it. You guys are assuming in like, great shape ... you've reached a level that is, is I want to be at that level. So, so yeah, that's why that's why I'm reaching out.
anchors.note: The entire reason he is on the call is Trevor personally — his videos, his philosophy, his physique. This is the strongest price-supporting asset available, and it is precisely what the $3,000 tier removes. He probed the substitute coach's credibility within seconds: 'Does his head coach have a channel or a YouTube channel or anything like that?'

unmet_demand.want: To see the programme, or a sample of it, before committing $6,000
unmet_demand.why_unmet: There is no trial, preview, sample week or structured walkthrough to offer. The only answer available to the rep was the try-it-to-know-it reframe. For a buyer who has never purchased coaching and whose objection is a first-time spending threshold, the absence of anything to inspect is a live commercial cost.

unmet_demand.want: Live human coaching interaction rather than asynchronous form-based check-ins
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The rep described the mechanics accurately: one 30-45 minute onboarding call with Trevor, then video form feedback and an in-app weekly check-in form — 'no need to actually getting on a call with him'. The prospect had been picturing something closer to in-person coaching, and the price objection surfaced immediately afterwards. The programme genuinely does not include recurring live sessions.

unmet_demand.want: Trevor specifically, since Trevor's videos and philosophy are why he made contact
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The half-price tier substitutes head coach Caden for Trevor while being described as 'everything is almost the same'. Trevor's personal credibility is the asset this buyer is actually purchasing, and the cheaper tier removes it without any credibility being established for the replacement — the rep's only supporting evidence was his own experience of being coached by Caden.

Raised as a genuine difficulty and deferred rather than answered — the rep said 'that's going to be a little tricky with the protein intake. So definitely Trevor needs to address that', then floated more fish and vegetarian protein shakes. It is unclear from the call whether the nutrition system has a worked vegetarian pathway or whether it would be improvised per client.

unmet_demand.want: Help with an all-or-nothing perfectionist psychology that resets him to zero after any disruption
unmet_demand.why_unmet: This is his actual root cause, he named it himself, and the rep agreed it was the target. The offer addresses it only indirectly, through programme flexibility and a coach who will adjust the week. Whether a strength coach is the right provider for what the prospect describes as 'these counterproductive moods that I get into' is genuinely unclear and was never examined.
